maths_ocr_h.11.1.summary: Mastering the interpretation and representation of data at OCR GCSE Higher tier requires absolute precision in constructing and reading advanced statistical diagrams. You must fluently transition between bar charts, pie charts, dual and composite bar charts, stem-and-leaf diagrams, frequency polygons, histograms with unequal class widths, cumulative frequency diagrams, and box plots. Securing a grade 9 depends on not just drawing shapes accurately, but extracting exact statistical measures, calculating missing frequencies from density, and interpreting complex distributions under exam conditions.

core.h: Bar Charts and Comparative Bar Charts
core.p: Bar charts display categorical or discrete data using rectangular bars where the height is proportional to the frequency. For comparing two sets of data on the same categories, dual or composite (stacked) bar charts are used.
bullets: Bars must be of equal width with equal spaces between them on the horizontal axis.
The vertical axis must start at zero and have a linear, evenly spaced scale.
Dual bar charts place two bars side-by-side for each category with a key to distinguish them.
Composite bar charts stack data components vertically within a single bar to show totals and proportions simultaneously.

callouts.p: Always start the frequency axis at zero. Starting higher exaggerates differences and loses marks.
Forgetting to leave equal gaps between bars on discrete scales is an automatic loss of accuracy marks.

fig.cap: A dual bar chart comparing two groups across four categories with clear spacing and a mandatory legend.

core.p: Pie charts represent proportions of a whole using sectors of a circle. The angle of each sector is proportional to the frequency of that category.
bullets: Calculate sector angles using the formula: Angle = (Frequency / Total Frequency) x 360 degrees.
Check accuracy by ensuring all sector angles sum to exactly 360 degrees.
Always label each sector clearly with its category name or percentage.
When given a pie chart with sector angles and one absolute frequency, find the multiplier 360 / Total Angle or Frequency / Angle to find other values.

callouts.p: Sum your calculated angles before drawing. If they do not equal 360, recompute immediately.

core.p: Stem-and-leaf diagrams display numerical data while retaining the original data values, ordered sequentially and split into a stem and a leaf.
bullets: A mandatory key must be included, e.g., '3 | 2 means 32'.
Leaves must be single digits, sorted in ascending order from left to right for each stem.
Stems must be consecutive integers, even if a stem has no corresponding leaves (leave the row blank).
Back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagrams allow direct visual comparison of two datasets sharing the same central stem column.

callouts.p: An explanatory statement defining how to read the digits, without which zero marks are awarded.

core.p: Frequency polygons connect the midpoints of the top of each class interval with straight lines to show continuous data trends and allow comparisons.
bullets: Plot each point at the midpoint of the class interval on the x-axis and the frequency on the y-axis.
Midpoint = (Lower Bound + Upper Bound) / 2.
Connect adjacent points with straight line segments (do not draw curves).
Anchor the polygon by extending the line down to the x-axis at the midpoint of the class interval before the first data class and after the last data class.

callouts.p: Failing to attach both ends of the frequency polygon to the baseline x-axis loses accuracy marks.

core.p: Histograms display continuous grouped data where the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency. They are required when class intervals are unequal.
bullets: Frequency Density = Frequency / Class Width.
The vertical axis is always labelled 'Frequency Density', never 'Frequency'.
Class width is Upper Bound minus Lower Bound.
Area of bar = Frequency Density x Class Width = Frequency.

callouts.p: In a histogram, height does not equal frequency. Frequency equals area (Height x Width).

core.p: Exam questions frequently require finding missing frequencies, estimating numbers of items within a sub-interval, or reconstructing frequency tables from histograms.
bullets: To find frequency from a given bar, calculate Area = Height (Frequency Density) x Width.
If a scale is missing on the vertical axis, use a known frequency and its bar dimensions to deduce the scale factor.
To estimate how many values lie within a partial interval, assume uniform distribution within that class interval and calculate proportional areas.
Always check boundary values carefully when intervals overlap (e.g., 10-20 and 20-30).

callouts.p: Find the area of the easiest bar first to establish your frequency-to-square ratio.

core.p: Cumulative frequency tracks the running total of frequencies as values increase, allowing us to estimate median, quartiles, and percentiles.
bullets: Construct a cumulative frequency column by successively adding frequencies down the table.
Always plot cumulative frequency points at the UPPER boundary of each class interval, not the midpoint.
Join the plotted points with a smooth, continuous increasing S-shaped curve (never use straight line segments between points).
Start the curve at zero cumulative frequency on the lower boundary of the first interval.

callouts.p: Plot at (Upper Class Boundary, Cumulative Frequency).
Connecting cumulative frequency points with a ruler loses marks; it must be a smooth freehand curve.

fig.cap: A cumulative frequency S-curve showing upper boundary plotting and quartile estimation lines.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="40" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 50 200 Q 150 195 210 130 T 350 45" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="120" x2="205" y2="120" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/><line x1="205" y1="200" x2="205" y2="120" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/><text x="25" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">50</text><text x="190" y="215" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Median</text></svg>

core.p: Box plots provide a graphical summary of a dataset based on its five-figure summary: minimum, lower quartile (Q1), median (Q2), upper quartile (Q3), and maximum.
bullets: The five-figure summary values are: Lowest value, Q1, Median, Q3, Highest value.
The box spans from Q1 to Q3, with a vertical line inside representing the median.
Whiskers extend from the ends of the box to the minimum and maximum values.
Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1, representing the spread of the middle 50% of data.

callouts.p: Be meticulous with scale divisions when reading values off the axis for Q1, median, and Q3.

core.p: Higher tier OCR questions require comparing two distributions using statistical diagrams (such as box plots or cumulative frequency curves). Comparisons must reference both location and spread.
bullets: Location comparison: Use Median or Mean. State which dataset has a higher or lower average and interpret in context.
Spread comparison: Use Interquartile Range (IQR) or Range. State which dataset is more consistent or more variable.
Never give vague statements like 'Group A is higher'; specify 'The median weight for Group A (34 kg) is greater than for Group B (28 kg)'.
Always write comparisons in the context of the question (units and variable names included).

callouts.p: Every comparison mark scheme requires two things: a numerical statistic and a contextual statement.

core.p: Scatter diagrams plot pairs of numerical observations (bivariate data) on a cartesian grid to investigate potential relationships between two variables.
bullets: One variable is on the x-axis (independent) and the other on the y-axis (dependent).
Describe correlation as positive, negative, or none, qualified by strong or moderate.
Line of best fit: A straight line that minimizes the distance of points above and below it, passing through the mean point (mean x, mean y).
Interpolation (estimating within data range) is reliable; extrapolation (estimating outside data range) is unreliable.

callouts.p: Correlation does not imply causation. Two variables may correlate due to a third confounding variable.

fig.cap: A scatter diagram showing positive correlation and a line of best fit.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="40" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="80" cy="170" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="110" cy="150" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="140" cy="130" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="180" cy="110" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="220" cy="90" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="270" cy="65" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><line x1="60" y1="185" x2="320" y2="55" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="230" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Variable X</text><text x="15" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540" transform="rotate(-90 15 120)">Variable Y</text></svg>

analogy.p: Representing data is like creating different types of geographical maps. A bar chart is a street map showing discrete landmarks, a histogram is a topographical relief map where height and area represent density and volume of terrain, and a box plot is a geological cross-section showing key elevation strata (min, quartiles, max). Where this analogy breaks down is that geographical maps preserve actual physical space, whereas statistical diagrams distort space to encode frequency, magnitude, and probability.

terms.d: Frequency divided by the class width, used as the height of bars in a histogram.
The running total of frequencies up to the upper boundary of each class interval.
The median of the lower half of a dataset, representing the 25th percentile (n/4th value).
The median of the upper half of a dataset, representing the 75th percentile (3n/4th value).
The difference between the upper quartile and lower quartile (Q3 - Q1), measuring spread.
The minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum of a dataset.
The difference between the upper class boundary and the lower class boundary.
A line graph joining midpoints of class intervals to frequencies.
A table displaying numerical data split into leading digits (stems) and trailing digits (leaves).
Data involving pairs of numerical observations on two different variables.
Estimating an unknown value within the range of known data points.
Estimating an unknown value outside the range of known data points, which is less reliable.

mistakes.w: Plotting cumulative frequency points at class midpoints.
mistakes.r: Always plot cumulative frequency points at the upper class boundary.

mistakes.w: Using frequency on the vertical axis of a histogram with unequal class widths.
mistakes.r: The vertical axis must be frequency density (Frequency / Class Width).

mistakes.w: Connecting cumulative frequency points with straight line segments.
mistakes.r: Draw a smooth, continuous S-shaped curve through the points.

mistakes.w: Comparing datasets by mentioning only averages without discussing spread.
mistakes.r: Always compare both location (median/mean) and spread (IQR/range) with numerical values.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the stem-and-leaf key.
mistakes.r: A clear key explaining what a stem and leaf represent is mandatory.

mistakes.w: Anchoring frequency polygons to the origin (0,0) incorrectly.
mistakes.r: Anchor frequency polygons to the x-axis at midpoints of intervals one class below and above.

mistakes.w: Stating bar chart frequency axes must start at numbers other than zero.
mistakes.r: Frequency axes on bar charts must always start at zero.

exam.q: A histogram has a bar for the interval 10 <= x < 25 with a width of 15 and a height of 4. Calculate the frequency for this interval.
model: Frequency = Frequency Density x Class Width
exam.tip: Remember frequency is the area of the bar in a histogram.

exam.q: Explain why extrapolation is less reliable than interpolation when using a scatter graph.
model: Extrapolation requires estimating outside the range of known data values
There is no evidence that the established trend or correlation continues outside this range.
exam.tip: Learn standard definitions for interpolation and extrapolation.

exam.q: From a cumulative frequency graph where n = 80, estimate the interquartile range.
model: Find Q1 at cumulative frequency 20 and read corresponding x value
Find Q3 at cumulative frequency 60 and read corresponding x value
Calculate IQR = Q3 - Q1
exam.tip: Quarterly marks are n/4 (Q1), 2n/4 (Median), and 3n/4 (Q3).

exam.q: Describe the comparison between two box plots representing test scores for Class A (Median 62, IQR 12) and Class B (Median 55, IQR 24).
model: Class A has a higher median (62 > 55), so on average Class A scored higher.
Class A has a lower IQR (12 < 24), so Class A scores are more consistent/less spread out than Class B.
exam.tip: Always give one statement about average/location and one about spread/consistency, both with numbers and context.

exam.q: A pie chart sector has an angle of 54 degrees and represents 18 students. Find the total number of students represented in the pie chart.
model: 360 / 54 = 6.666... or angle per student = 54 / 18 = 3 degrees per student
Total students = 360 / 3 = 120
exam.tip: Find the unit value (degrees per item) to solve pie chart reverse problems quickly.

exam.q: Construct the upper class boundary for the grouped frequency interval 20 < x <= 30 and state where to plot its cumulative frequency.
model: Upper boundary is 30
Plot cumulative frequency at (30, cumulative frequency)
exam.tip: Cumulative frequency is always plotted at the upper boundary.

exam.q: State two requirements for drawing a correct bar chart for discrete data.
model: Equal width of bars
Equal gaps between bars and frequency axis starting at zero
exam.tip: Check that your bars do not touch unless it is a histogram or grouped bar chart.

exam.q: A stem-and-leaf diagram has stem 4 and leaves 2, 5, 5, 8 with key '4 | 2 = 4.2 kg'. Write down the raw data values represented by this stem.
model: All values correctly extracted using the key
exam.tip: Check decimal placement carefully using the given key.

exam.q: Explain how to find the estimated median from a frequency table with grouped continuous data.
model: Find total frequency n and divide by 2 (n/2 position)
Construct a cumulative frequency column
Identify the class interval containing the (n/2)th value
exam.tip: For grouped data, we estimate the median; we do not find an exact value.

worked.q: The table shows the time, t minutes, taken by 100 runners to finish a race. Construct a cumulative frequency table and draw its curve to estimate the median time.
steps: Step 1: Create cumulative frequency by adding frequencies successively: 8, 8+22=30, 30+45=75, 75+20=95, 95+5=100.
Step 2: Plot points at upper boundaries: (20,8), (30,30), (40,75), (50,95), (60,100), starting at (10,0).
Step 3: Join with a smooth S-curve.
Step 4: Find median at n/2 = 50 on cumulative frequency axis, read across to curve and down to x-axis.

worked.q: A histogram has a class 0 <= x < 10 with frequency density 3 and class 10 <= x < 25 with frequency density 2. Find the total frequency for the range 0 <= x < 25.
steps: Step 1: Calculate frequency for first interval: Width = 10 - 0 = 10. Frequency = 3 x 10 = 30.
Step 2: Calculate frequency for second interval: Width = 25 - 10 = 15. Frequency = 2 x 15 = 30.
Step 3: Sum both frequencies to find total.

maths_ocr_h.11.2.summary: Mastering OCR GCSE Higher Statistics requires calculating exact summary statistics from raw, frequency, and grouped frequency data, while understanding how outliers distort measures. You must be able to draw, interpret, and interpolate from cumulative frequency diagrams, box plots, and scatter graphs to assess correlation and make reliable predictions. Additionally, critically evaluating statistical misrepresentation in graphs and misleading claims is essential for securing a grade 9.

core.p: Summary statistics provide single values to represent the centre and spread of a dataset. For raw data, the **mean** is found by summing all values and dividing by the count ($n$). The **median** is the middle value when data is ordered in magnitude, located at position $\frac{n+1}{2}$. The **mode** is the most frequent value. When data is presented in a frequency table, the mean is calculated using $\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$, where $x$ represents the midpoint for grouped data.
bullets: **Mean**: $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$ for raw data, and $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$ for frequency tables.
**Median**: Position is $\frac{n+1}{2}$. For grouped data, use linear interpolation.
**Mode/Modal Class**: The value or class interval with the highest frequency.
When data is open-ended (e.g., '10 or more'), exact means cannot be calculated without assuming a midpoint for the open class.

callouts.p: Use the median for skewed data or data with extreme outliers because it is not affected by extreme values. Use the mean when every value must be accounted for.

core.h: Measures of Spread: Range and Interquartile Range
core.p: Spread measures how dispersed or varied a dataset is. The **range** is simply the maximum value minus the minimum value, making it extremely sensitive to outliers. The **interquartile range (IQR)** measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data, calculated as the upper quartile ($Q_3$) minus the lower quartile ($Q_1$).
bullets: **Range** = Maximum value $-$ Minimum value.
**Lower Quartile ($Q_1$)**: Value at position $\frac{n+1}{4}$.
**Upper Quartile ($Q_3$)**: Value at position $\frac{3(n+1)}{4}$.
**Interquartile Range (IQR)** = $Q_3 - Q_1$.
IQR is a more robust measure of spread than the range because it ignores top and bottom 25% extremes.

callouts.p: The difference between the upper quartile and the lower quartile, representing the range of the middle 50% of data.

core.p: Cumulative frequency graphs display the running total of frequencies against the **upper class boundaries**. They are essential for estimating medians, quartiles, and percentiles for continuous or grouped data. Always plot points at the upper bound of each interval and join them with a smooth, continuous S-shaped curve (never straight line segments).
bullets: Plot points at **(upper class boundary, cumulative frequency)**.
Start the curve at the lower boundary of the first class with a cumulative frequency of zero.
To find the median ($Q_2$), go to $\frac{n}{2}$ on the vertical axis, read across to the curve, and drop down to read the value.
To find the IQR, subtract the value at $\frac{n}{4}$ ($Q_1$) from the value at $\frac{3n}{4}$ ($Q_3$).

callouts.p: Students often plot cumulative frequency points at interval midpoints. Points must always be plotted at the upper class boundary.

core.p: A box plot provides a visual summary of a dataset's distribution using five key values: minimum, lower quartile ($Q_1$), median ($Q_2$), upper quartile ($Q_3$), and maximum. They are drawn against a scaled number line and allow for immediate visual comparison of two or more datasets regarding central tendency and spread.
bullets: The five key values required are: **Minimum**, **$Q_1$**, **Median**, **$Q_3$**, and **Maximum**.
A box is drawn from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, with a vertical line inside the box representing the median.
Whiskers extend from the ends of the box to the minimum and maximum values.
To compare distributions, always comment on **average** (median) and **spread** (IQR), referencing the context of the question.

callouts.p: When comparing two box plots in exam questions, never just state numbers. Write: 'Dataset A has a higher median (15 vs 12), showing higher average performance, but a larger IQR (6 vs 4), showing less consistency.'

fig.cap: Structure of a standard box plot showing minimum, quartiles, median, and maximum.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="120" x2="350" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="90" x2="80" y2="150" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="320" y1="90" x2="320" y2="150" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="140" y="80" width="120" height="80" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="190" y1="80" x2="190" y2="160" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="120" x2="140" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="260" y1="120" x2="320" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="75" y="175" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Min</text><text x="130" y="175" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Q1</text><text x="180" y="70" fill="#dc2626" font-size="11">Median</text><text x="310" y="175" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Max</text></svg>

core.p: An outlier is an extreme data point that lies unusually far away from the rest of the dataset. Outliers can be caused by recording errors, measurement mistakes, or genuine extreme observations. In OCR exams, outliers are formally defined mathematically using quartiles and the interquartile range.
bullets: Standard Higher tier rule for outliers: Any value greater than $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ or less than $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ is an outlier.
When an outlier is identified, examiners may ask whether it should be removed. Mention that valid data should generally be kept unless it is a clear recording error.
Outliers heavily skew the mean and range, but have very little impact on the median and IQR.

callouts.p: Lower bound: $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. Upper bound: $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.

core.p: Bivariate data involves pairs of numerical observations for two variables on the same subjects (e.g., height and weight). A scatter graph plots these pairs as coordinates $(x, y)$. By analysing the pattern of points, we can determine if there is a relationship or **correlation** between the two variables.
bullets: **Positive correlation**: As $x$ increases, $y$ increases (points trend bottom-left to top-right).
**Negative correlation**: As $x$ increases, $y$ decreases (points trend top-left to bottom-right).
**No correlation**: Points are scattered randomly with no discernible linear trend.
Strength of correlation depends on how closely the points follow a straight line pattern.

callouts.p: Never state that variable A *causes* variable B just because there is strong correlation. There may be a third confounding variable, or the relationship might be purely coincidental.

fig.cap: Scatter graph illustrating positive correlation and a line of best fit.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="80" cy="170" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="110" cy="150" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="150" cy="130" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="190" cy="100" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="240" cy="80" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="300" cy="50" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><line x1="60" y1="190" x2="340" y2="40" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-dasharray="4" stroke-width="2"/><text x="160" y="225" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Variable X</text><text x="10" y="110" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Variable Y</text></svg>

core.p: A line of best fit is a straight line drawn on a scatter graph to represent the general trend of the bivariate data. A good line of best fit must pass through the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ and have roughly an equal number of points above and below the line.
bullets: Used to make predictions for unknown values of $y$ given $x$ (or vice versa).
Must be drawn with a ruler across the full range of data.
**Interpolation**: Predicting a value *within* the range of given data points (reliable).
**Extrapolation**: Predicting a value *outside* the range of given data points (unreliable, as the trend may change).

callouts.p: Examiners check that your line of best fit is balanced. Do not simply connect the first and last points unless they happen to represent the statistical average trend.

core.p: Graphs and statistics can be deliberately or accidentally manipulated to mislead the reader. In exam questions, you must be able to spot and explain flaws in graphical representations and summary claims.
bullets: **Broken or omitted axes**: The vertical axis does not start at zero, exaggerating differences between categories.
**Inconsistent scale**: Unequal intervals on axes distort the visual rate of change.
**Missing labels or units**: Makes charts impossible to interpret accurately.
**Area/Volume distortion**: Scaling 2D pictograms or 3D bars where doubling the height doubles both dimensions, exaggerating the visual volume by a factor of four or eight.

callouts.p: Always check if the y-axis starts at zero. If it doesn't, small differences look massive, which is a classic exam trap.

analogy.p: Imagine timing 1,000 runners in a massive marathon. The **mean** is the average time of everyone combined, which can be massively delayed if an elite runner breaks a leg and crawls across in 10 hours (an **outlier**). The **median** is simply the time of the 500th runner to cross the line, completely unaffected by how slowly the last runner finishes. A **box plot** gives you a snapshot of the race: the start time of the fastest finisher (min), where the quarter-way runners are ($Q_1$), the halfway champion (median), the three-quarter mark ($Q_3$), and the slowest finisher (max). **Interpolation** is guessing a runner's split time at the 20-mile mark based on their overall pace, whereas **extrapolation** is foolishly predicting how long they would take to run 50 miles based on those 26.2 miles.

terms.d: Values that summarise the central tendency and spread of a dataset.
The sum of all values divided by the total number of values.
The middle value when data is arranged in ascending order.
The most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
The difference between the upper quartile ($Q_3$) and lower quartile ($Q_1$).
The running total of frequencies up to a given upper class boundary.
A graphical representation of data using minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum.
A data point that lies significantly outside the overall pattern of distribution, defined as $> Q_3 + 1.5\text{IQR}$ or $< Q_1 - 1.5\text{IQR}$.
Data which has pairs of values for two different variables.
A measure of the relationship or association between two variables.
Estimating a value within the range of measured data points using a line of best fit.
Estimating a value outside the range of measured data points, which is generally unreliable.

mistakes.w: Plotting cumulative frequency at the midpoint of class intervals.
mistakes.r: Always plot cumulative frequency points at the upper class boundary.

mistakes.w: Calculating IQR as Max minus Min.
mistakes.r: IQR is Upper Quartile ($Q_3$) minus Lower Quartile ($Q_1$).

mistakes.w: Stating that strong correlation proves causation.
mistakes.r: Correlation only shows a relationship; it does not prove that one variable causes the other.

mistakes.w: Finding the median position as n/2 instead of (n+1)/2 for raw data lists.
mistakes.r: Position of raw data median is (n+1)/2. For grouped frequency tables, use n/2 with cumulative frequency.

mistakes.w: Drawing a line of best fit by connecting the first and last data points.
mistakes.r: A line of best fit must be balanced by eye, having roughly equal points above and below, and passing through the mean point.

mistakes.w: Saying extrapolation is completely accurate because it uses a mathematical line.
mistakes.r: Extrapolation is unreliable because the trend may not continue outside the tested range.

mistakes.w: Forgetting units when describing summary statistics in context.
mistakes.r: Always include proper context units (e.g., grams, seconds, pounds) in your final answers.

exam.q: The lower quartile of a dataset is 12 and the upper quartile is 44. Calculate the interquartile range.
exam.tip: Subtract lower quartile from upper quartile.

exam.q: Explain why a vertical axis starting at 50 instead of 0 can be misleading in a bar chart.
model: It exaggerates the differences between bar heights
making small proportional changes look much larger than they actually are.
exam.tip: Mention exaggeration and proportionality.

exam.q: A dataset of 40 values has $\sum fx = 680$. Calculate the estimated mean.
exam.tip: Use the formula sum of fx divided by sum of f.

exam.q: The median of 35 items of data is required. State the position of the median item.
exam.tip: Remember (n+1)/2 for raw data.

exam.q: State the difference between interpolation and extrapolation on a scatter graph.
model: Interpolation estimates values within the range of given data points
whereas extrapolation estimates values outside the range.
exam.tip: Keep definitions concise and precise.

exam.q: A box plot has minimum 5, Q1 12, median 20, Q3 35, and maximum 45. Determine if 70 is an outlier using the 1.5 x IQR rule.
model: Since 70 is greater than 69.5,
70 is an outlier.
exam.tip: Show all calculation steps clearly for the upper threshold.

exam.q: Describe the type of correlation shown when as temperature increases, ice cream sales increase.
model: Positive correlation
exam.tip: State positive or negative clearly.

exam.q: Explain why a researcher should be cautious when using a line of best fit to predict a value far beyond the collected data range.
model: This is extrapolation,
and the trend may not continue in the same way outside the known data range.
exam.tip: Use the term extrapolation and explain the risk.

exam.q: Give one reason why the median is preferred over the mean when analysing house prices.
model: House prices have extreme high outliers (mansions) which skew the mean, whereas the median is unaffected.
exam.tip: Mention skewed data and extreme outliers.

worked.q: The table shows the time taken, t minutes, by 80 people to solve a puzzle. Time (0 < t <= 10): frequency 10; (10 < t <= 20): frequency 24; (20 < t <= 30): frequency 30; (30 < t <= 40): frequency 16. Calculate an estimate for the mean time.
steps: Find the midpoint (x) for each interval: 5, 15, 25, 35.
Multiply each midpoint by its frequency (fx): (10*5=50), (24*15=360), (30*25=750), (16*35=560).
Sum the fx values: 50 + 360 + 750 + 560 = 1720.
Divide by total frequency (80): 1720 / 80 = 21.5.

worked.q: A student records the exam scores of 60 pupils. Lower quartile Q1 = 32, Upper quartile Q3 = 68. Show that a score of 122 is an outlier.
steps: Calculate the interquartile range: IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 68 - 32 = 36.
Calculate the upper outlier threshold: Q3 + 1.5 * IQR = 68 + 1.5(36).
Evaluate: 1.5 * 36 = 54, so threshold = 68 + 54 = 122.
Compare: Since the score is 122 (or greater than/equal to the upper threshold boundary), it is classified as an outlier.
worked.ans: Threshold is 122, so 122 is an outlier.

maths_ocr_h.11.0.summary: Sampling is the process of selecting a subset of individuals from a larger group (the population) to make inferences about that group. A **sample** must be representative, which is achieved through **simple random sampling** where every member has an equal chance of selection. Any systematic error that skews results is called **bias**, and recognising and avoiding bias is essential for valid conclusions in statistics.

core.p: In statistics a population is the complete set of items or individuals that you are interested in studying. It can be finite (e.g., all pupils in a school) or conceptually infinite (e.g., all possible outcomes of a dice roll).
bullets: Denoted by the symbol **N**.
All characteristics of interest are called parameters (e.g., μ, σ).
Often impossible to measure directly, so we use a sample.

callouts.p: The entire set of objects or events that satisfy a set of criteria.

core.p: A sample is a smaller collection taken from the population that we actually observe or measure. It allows us to estimate population parameters using statistics.
bullets: Denoted by the symbol **n**.
Statistics (e.g., ̅x, s) are calculated from the sample.
The quality of a sample determines the reliability of any inference.

callouts.p: A subset of a population selected for measurement.

core.p: SRS is the gold‑standard method for obtaining an unbiased sample. Every individual in the population has an equal probability of being chosen, and each possible sample of size n is equally likely.
bullets: Can be performed with a random number table, calculator, or computer.
Requires a complete and up‑to‑date sampling frame (a list of all population members).
If the population is very large, a **simple random sample without replacement** is usually assumed.

callouts.p: Equal chance for every member → unbiased estimate of parameters.
Check the exam question: if it says ‘randomly selected’, assume SRS unless otherwise stated.

core.p: Because it minimises systematic error, allowing the sample statistics to be unbiased estimators of the population parameters.
bullets: Law of Large Numbers works best with SRS.
Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are derived assuming SRS.
Reduces the risk of **selection bias**.

callouts.p: Do NOT confuse ‘random’ with ‘representative’; a random sample can still be unrepresentative by chance, especially if n is small.

core.p: Bias is any systematic error that leads a sample to over‑ or under‑represent parts of the population, causing the sample statistic to deviate from the true parameter.
bullets: Types of bias include:
• **Selection bias** – certain groups are more likely to be chosen.
• **Non‑response bias** – people who do not respond differ from those who do.
• **Measurement bias** – the instrument or method consistently mis‑records values.
Bias cannot be corrected by increasing the sample size.

callouts.p: A systematic error that leads to an inaccurate representation of the population.

core.p: Examiners expect you to name at least two ways to reduce bias when designing a study.
bullets: Use a complete and up‑to‑date sampling frame.
Employ simple random sampling or stratified random sampling when appropriate.
Ensure high response rates (follow‑ups, incentives).
Standardise measurement procedures and calibrate equipment.

callouts.p: In mark‑scheme, each valid method you list gains one mark (up to the maximum for the question).

core.p: A sampling frame is a list of all members of the population from which the sample is drawn. It must be as accurate as possible.
bullets: If the frame omits some members, **coverage bias** occurs.
Examples: school roll‑call, electoral register, customer database.

callouts.p: A complete list of all elements in the population.

core.p: Larger samples tend to give more reliable estimates, but size alone does not guarantee lack of bias.
bullets: Rule of thumb for proportion estimates: n ≥ 30 and n(1‑p) ≥ 30.
For means, the Central Limit Theorem applies when n ≥ 30 (higher tier).
Even with n = 200, a biased selection will still give a biased result.

callouts.p: Do not claim a large n removes bias – it only reduces random error.

core.p: Sampling underpins every later topic: summary statistics, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and bivariate analysis all assume a well‑designed sample.
bullets: If the sample is biased, any calculated mean, median, standard deviation, or correlation will be misleading.
Understanding sampling helps you critique data presented in the media.

core.p: For higher‑tier questions you may be asked to evaluate the suitability of a sampling method, discussing both random error and bias.
bullets: State the **advantage** of SRS (unbiased, simple to analyse).
State a **limitation** (may be impractical for very large populations).
Compare with **stratified sampling** – reduces sampling error when sub‑groups differ markedly.
Use the terms *random error*, *systematic error*, *bias*, *representativeness*.

callouts.p: Higher‑tier marks often come from a clear, balanced evaluation.

analogy.t: Sampling is like tasting a soup to decide if it needs salt.
analogy.p: Imagine a huge pot of soup (the population). You can’t drink the whole pot, so you take a spoonful (the sample). If you stir the pot well and take the spoonful at random, the taste will reflect the whole soup – this is simple random sampling. If you always scoop from the top, you might miss the flavours that settle at the bottom – that’s bias. The analogy breaks down because taste is subjective and a single spoonful may not capture subtle flavours, just as a very small sample may give a misleading estimate despite being random.

terms.d: The entire set of individuals or items that satisfy the criteria of a study.
A subset of the population selected for measurement.
A sampling method where every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected and every possible sample of a given size is equally likely.
A complete list of all members of the population from which a sample is drawn.
A systematic error that leads to an inaccurate representation of the population.
Bias that occurs when some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others.
Bias arising when the individuals who do not respond differ in relevant ways from those who do.
Bias caused by faulty measurement instruments or procedures.
Variability in sample results that occurs by chance and can be reduced by increasing sample size.
The degree to which a sample reflects the characteristics of the population.
Bias introduced when the sampling frame does not include all elements of the population.
A method where the population is divided into sub‑groups (strata) and random samples are taken from each stratum.

mistakes.w: ‘Random’ automatically means the sample is representative.
mistakes.r: Random sampling reduces bias but does not guarantee representativeness, especially with small n.

mistakes.w: Increasing sample size removes bias.
mistakes.r: Bias is systematic; larger n only reduces random error.

mistakes.w: Using a convenience sample is acceptable if the sample is large.
mistakes.r: Convenience samples are prone to selection bias regardless of size.

mistakes.w: ‘Sampling frame’ and ‘population’ are interchangeable.
mistakes.r: The frame is a list of the population; if it is incomplete, bias occurs.

mistakes.w: All samples are unbiased if taken from the whole population.
mistakes.r: Bias can still arise from non‑response or measurement errors.

mistakes.w: Stratified sampling is the same as simple random sampling.
mistakes.r: Stratified sampling involves dividing the population into groups first; it is a different technique.

mistakes.w: If a question says ‘selected at random’, you can assume no bias.
mistakes.r: You must still consider possible sources of bias such as incomplete frames or non‑response.

mistakes.w: Bias only affects the mean, not other statistics.
mistakes.r: Bias affects any statistic that estimates a population parameter.

mistakes.w: A sample of 5 is always too small to be useful.
mistakes.r: For very small populations, a sample of 5 may be appropriate; the key is representativeness, not a fixed number.

mistakes.w: Random number tables are outdated and not needed in exams.
mistakes.r: Examiners accept any valid method of random selection, including tables, calculators or software.

exam.q: A school has 800 pupils. To find the average height, the teacher randomly selects 40 pupils using a random number generator. Explain why this method is likely to give an unbiased estimate of the true mean height.
model: All 800 pupils are listed in a sampling frame (the school roll).
Each pupil has an equal chance of being chosen (simple random sampling).
Therefore no particular group (e.g., taller or shorter pupils) is systematically over‑ or under‑represented.
An unbiased estimator means the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean.
exam.tip: State the equal‑chance principle and link it to the definition of unbiasedness.

exam.q: Identify two possible sources of bias if the same teacher instead asked the class captain to choose 40 pupils he thought were ‘representative’.
model: Selection bias – the captain may pick friends or pupils he knows, not a random cross‑section.
Subjective bias – personal judgement may favour certain heights, ages, etc.
exam.tip: Use the exact terms ‘selection bias’ and ‘subjective bias’.

exam.q: A researcher uses an online questionnaire sent to all members of a club. Only 30 % respond. Discuss how non‑response bias could affect the results.
model: Non‑response bias occurs when those who do not answer differ from respondents.
If non‑respondents are, for example, less active members, the sample will over‑represent active members.
This systematic difference leads to estimates (e.g., average attendance) that are higher than the true club average.
Increasing response rate (reminders, incentives) can reduce this bias.
Even with a large sample size, the bias remains because it is systematic.
Hence conclusions drawn without accounting for non‑response may be misleading.
exam.tip: Structure answer: definition → effect → mitigation → link to systematic nature.

exam.q: State one advantage and one limitation of simple random sampling.
model: Advantage: It provides an unbiased sample because every member has an equal chance of selection.
Limitation: It can be impractical for very large populations if a complete sampling frame is unavailable.
exam.tip: Use the exact wording ‘unbiased’ and ‘impractical for large populations’.

exam.q: Explain why a larger sample size does not eliminate bias, using an example.
model: Bias is a systematic error, not random variation.
If a sample is drawn from an incomplete frame that omits all pupils from Year 12, increasing n from 30 to 300 still excludes Year 12 pupils.
Therefore the sample statistic will remain biased regardless of size.
Only correcting the source of bias (e.g., using a complete frame) removes it.
exam.tip: Contrast bias with random error; give a concrete example.

exam.q: A poll of 500 voters is taken using stratified sampling with equal numbers from each age group. Explain how this method reduces sampling error compared with simple random sampling.
model: Stratified sampling ensures each age group is represented proportionally.
If some age groups have very different voting patterns, SRS might under‑sample a small but distinct group, increasing variability.
By guaranteeing representation, the variability between samples (sampling error) is reduced.
Hence estimates (e.g., overall voting intention) are more precise.
exam.tip: Mention ‘representation of sub‑groups’ and ‘reduces variability’.

exam.q: Define the term ‘sampling frame’ and give one reason why an inaccurate frame leads to bias.
model: A sampling frame is a complete list of all members of the population.
If the frame omits certain individuals, those groups cannot be selected, causing coverage bias.
exam.tip: Use the exact phrase ‘coverage bias’.

exam.q: A researcher draws a sample of 50 from a population of 200 by selecting every 4th name on an alphabetical list. Identify the type of bias, if any, and justify your answer.
model: This is systematic sampling, not simple random sampling.
If the list is ordered by height, selecting every 4th name could over‑represent a particular height range – a form of selection bias.
Therefore the method can introduce bias unless the ordering is random with respect to the variable of interest.
exam.tip: State that bias depends on the ordering; link to selection bias.

exam.q: Discuss why it is important to consider bias when interpreting a graph that shows the average test scores of a sample of schools.
model: If the sample of schools was not randomly selected, it may over‑represent high‑performing schools (selection bias).
Any conclusions about the national average would therefore be too high.
Bias can also arise from non‑response if schools with low scores chose not to submit data.
Recognising bias alerts the reader that the graph may not reflect the true population trend.
It may suggest the need for caution or for additional data collection.
Thus, evaluating bias is essential for accurate interpretation and decision‑making.
exam.tip: Link bias to the reliability of the graph’s conclusions.

worked.q: A university has a list of 1 200 students. Using a random number table, a researcher selects 60 students. Calculate the probability that a particular student is chosen.
steps: Total number of students N = 1 200.
Sample size n = 60.
Probability for any one student = n / N = 60 / 1 200.
Therefore the probability is 0.05 (or 5 %).

worked.q: From a population of 500 households, a simple random sample of 25 is taken. Explain why the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
steps: In simple random sampling each household has equal chance of selection.
All possible samples of size 25 are equally likely.
The expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean (by definition of unbiasedness).
Thus the sample mean does not systematically over‑ or under‑estimate the true mean.
worked.ans: Because SRS gives each household equal chance, the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, making it an unbiased estimator.

worked.q: A survey of 200 people is conducted by telephone. Only 150 people answer. Identify the type of bias and suggest one method to reduce it.
steps: Non‑response bias occurs because 50 people did not answer.
Those who did not answer may differ in the variable of interest.
To reduce it, the researcher could call back at different times or offer an incentive to increase response rate.
worked.ans: Non‑response bias; reduce by follow‑up calls or incentives to improve response rate.
